01 / THE QUESTION

What needed to work?

Watching a recording and playing a reconstructed game are different tasks. Takeover requires an explicit state and a model that can continue without future ball positions.

A seven-stage pipeline from capture and tracking through contact extraction, physics fitting, reconstruction, takeover and verification.

03 / THE ENGINEERING

The decision behind it.

Fit on the chronological first 60% of observations. For continuous replay, start from one observed seed and recorded paddle controls; do not resynchronize future ball states.

  1. 01Capture & tracking
  2. 02Contact extraction
  3. 03Physics fitting
  4. 04Replay & player takeover
  • Implemented capture, object tracking, contact extraction, physics fitting, reconstruction, takeover, and verification.
  • Fitted motion and collision parameters on the first 60% of observations.
  • Evaluated later-frame forecasts and continuous replay on five synthetic fixtures.
  • Added human-assisted detection corrections, deterministic input replay, and standalone offline game ZIP exports.

04 / THE EVIDENCE

What the work demonstrates.

The preview renders the actual exported Staggered scene. The fitted model starts from one observed state; it does not reset future ball positions to the footage.

0.65 pxmean ball-position error
1.26 px95th-percentile error
296scored frames

Preserved Staggered synthetic fixture: a continuous model replay from seed frame 4, using recorded paddle controls. Errors are relative to the observed tracks, not hidden ground truth. This single fixture does not establish performance on real gameplay footage.

Inspect the original report ↗

05 / THE BOUNDARIES

What I can stand behind.

The source clip is a synthetic fixture. Uploaded-video reconstruction supports a bounded fixed-camera Breakout family; real-game generalization remains unvalidated.

Building something useful means being precise about what it does, what has been checked, and what still needs to be tested.
